item.mechanism: High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution against irradiation-induced phase separation.
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature, fluences up to 1 × 10^16 cm^-2 (~43 dpa)
item.supporting_observation: No precipitates were observed in the single-phase alloy even at the highest fluence, whereas multiphase alloys showed extensive precipitation.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for multiphase HEAs (x=0.75, 1.5) where phase separation reduces configurational entropy; not tested at elevated temperatures where other phenomena like void swelling may occur.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the lack of precipitation might be due to precipitate size being too small to detect, but concluded it is due to phase stability.
quotes: the excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion
reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrains the formation of precipitate

item.mechanism: Sluggish atomic diffusion kinetically restrains the formation and growth of precipitates by suppressing solute mobility required for segregation.
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature
item.supporting_observation: The single-phase alloy exhibited great resistance to precipitation, attributed to the low mobility of atoms in the multicomponent equiatomic solid solution.
item.scope_limits: Specific to single-phase HEAs; the authors note that multiphase alloys do not exhibit this low atomic mobility to the same extent.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered the effects of other minor constituents but assumed they could be neglected to simplify the model.
quotes: Another reason for the great resistance of single phase HEA to precipitation may be the sluggish atomic diffusion
atomic diffusion in multicomponent HEA is suppressed, resulting in a very low mobility
only single phase HEAs are of the low atomic mobilities, leading to the great resistance to precipitation under ion irradiation

item.mechanism: Phase separation and formation of ordered phases reduce system configurational entropy, causing multiphase HEAs to behave like conventional immiscible binary or ternary alloys under irradiation.
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature, fluences up to 1 × 10^16 cm^-2
item.supporting_observation: Numerous coherent precipitates were observed in both multiphase HEAs, contrasting with the stability of the single-phase alloy.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to single-phase HEAs; the mechanism relies on the assumption that each phase can be treated as a binary or ternary alloy.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that interaction between different phases or grain boundaries might influence the process but assumed these effects could be neglected.
quotes: For the multiphase HEAs, the phase separations and formation of ordered phases reduce the system configurational entropy
resulting in the similar precipitation behavior with corresponding binary or ternary conventional alloys
the formation of ordered phases and phase separation reduce their configurational entropies, resulting in that they behave like conventional binary and ternary alloys

item.mechanism: Positive mixing enthalpy in specific phase compositions (e.g., Fe-Cr) provides the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation under irradiation.
item.system: A2 phases (Fe-Cr rich) and fcc phases in Al1.5CoCrFeNi and Al0.75CoCrFeNi
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature
item.supporting_observation: Precipitates enriched in Fe were observed in A2 and fcc phases, consistent with the positive mixing enthalpy of Fe-Cr.
item.scope_limits: Specific to phases with positive mixing enthalpy; does not explain precipitation in B2 phases where mixing enthalpies are negative.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors noted that in many Fe-Cr materials precipitates are enriched with Cr, but in this study they are enriched with Fe due to high Cr content.
quotes: It can be observed that the mixing enthalpy for Fe-Cr is very positive, which provides the thermodynamic driving force for the precipitation in A2 and fcc phases
the thermodynamic instability provides the driving force for the precipitation under ion irradiation
similar with the precipitation behavior of many immiscible binary systems

item.mechanism: Negative mixing enthalpies (e.g., Ni-Al, Co-Al) combined with positive Ni-Co enthalpy drive the precipitation of Co in B2 phases.
item.system: B2 phases (Al-Ni-Co rich) in Al0.75CoCrFeNi and Al1.5CoCrFeNi
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature
item.supporting_observation: Precipitates in B2 phases were found to contain a higher concentration of Co compared to the Al-rich matrix.
item.scope_limits: Specific to B2 phases; the mechanism explains why precipitate sizes in B2 phases are smaller than in A2 phases.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that lower atomic mobilities or smaller thermodynamic driving force might induce smaller precipitate sizes in B2 phases.
quotes: For the B2 phases, both mixing enthalpies of Ni-Al and Co-Al are very negative
the mixing enthalpy of Ni-Co is the most positive between the five alloying components, which provides the thermodynamic drive for the precipitation of Co in the irradiation

item.mechanism: Irradiation-induced defects (excess vacancies or mobile interstitials) enhance the kinetics of nucleation by promoting solute segregation at defect sinks.
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature
item.supporting_observation: The formation of precipitates is attributed to fluxes of irradiation-induced defects resulting in solute depletion or segregation at sinks.
item.scope_limits: The authors note that the specific mechanism of interstitial absorption by Fe is proposed but not directly measured in this study.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the interaction between different phases might play a role but assumed it could be neglected.
quotes: The generation of excess vacancies or mobile interstitials from damage cascade events can enhance the kinetics of nucleation
nucleation centers preferentially absorb the interstitials of Fe, promoting the growth of precipitates
The formation of precipitates in the ion irradiation is attributed to the fluxes of irradiation-induced defects

item.mechanism: Precipitate coalescence is the primary mechanism for the growth of precipitates in A2 phases of Al1.5CoCrFeNi with increasing fluence.
item.operating_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature, fluences from 5 × 10^15 to 1 × 10^16 cm^-2
item.supporting_observation: The precipitates in the A2 phases exhibited distinct growth with increasing fluence, which the authors attribute to coalescence.
item.scope_limits: Specific to A2 phases; the growth in B2 phases is described as slow and approaching saturation, not primarily driven by coalescence.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the growth might be due to other mechanisms but explicitly linked the distinct growth in A2 phases to coalescence.
quotes: The precipitates in the A2 phases of Al 1.5 CoCrFeNi exhibit a distinct growth with increasing fluence, which is mainly due to the precipitate coalescence
These coherent precipitates can easily coalesce with each other under continuous growth
below 5 × 10^15 cm^-2 no precipitate can be observed in HAADF or BF images

item.mechanism: High temperature irradiation responses differ drastically from room temperature, potentially involving void swelling and grain boundary segregation not observed at room temperature.
item.system: General HEAs (implied comparison to current study)
item.operating_conditions: Elevated temperatures (specifically mentioned as 500 °C in cited works), contrasting with room temperature irradiation in this study
item.supporting_observation: The authors note that irradiation-induced voids and segregation observed in other studies at high temperatures were not observed in their room temperature study.
item.scope_limits: The current study was conducted at room temperature; the mechanism of high-temperature behavior is not tested but inferred from literature.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors suggest that further systematic studies are required for applications in advanced nuclear systems at elevated temperatures.
quotes: These experimental phenomena are not observed in current study, indicating the irradiation responses of HEA at high temperatures are drastically different from that of room temperature
Further systematic studies on the irradiation responses of HEAs at elevated temperatures are required for their applications in advanced nuclear systems
K. Jin et al. [40] observed the irradiation-induced voids and its related volume swelling in various multi-component alloys at 500 °C
